item.title: I gave my PC a search tool that reads inside every document, and Windows Search can't compete
item.itunes:title: I gave my PC a search tool that reads inside every document, and Windows Search can't compete
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Some PC utilities solve problems I didn't even know had a better solution. DocFetcher is one such discovery. It's a free, open-source desktop application designed to make searching through large collections of documents easier. Unlike many tools that focus mainly on locating files, it puts document contents at the center of the search experience. I was curious to see how well it would fit into my daily workflow. So, I spent some time exploring its features, and there was more to it than I initially expected.

Windows Search couldn't find what I remembered reading

I remembered the contents, not the filename

I often remember reading something in a document but have no idea what I named the file or where I saved it. This happens quite often with my collection of downloaded PDFs, work documents, research material, and old notes. I usually start with Windows Search and type a few keywords I think might help. Sometimes, it works, but other times, I end up scrolling through unrelated results or trying different search terms without much luck.

The frustrating part is that I know the information is somewhere on my PC; I just can't get Windows to point me towards it. Renaming files and organizing folders helps to some extent, but it's not always practical when you deal with hundreds of documents. I wanted something that could make finding old information less of a guessing game.

DocFetcher turns scattered folders into a searchable library

Indexing the folders I actually need

Getting started with DocFetcher was fairly straightforward. After installing the desktop app, I created an index by right-clicking inside the search scope panel and selecting the folder I wanted to include. DocFetcher then scanned the selected location and built an index of its contents. I started with the Documents and Downloads folder rather than indexing my entire PC, which kept things manageable.

The initial process took a little time because I had quite a few files stored there, but I only had to wait for the first indexing pass to finish. Once it was ready, my selected folders became part of a dedicated search library. The best part is that more folders can be added whenever needed instead of starting everything from scratch.

DocFetcher also offers good control over what gets indexed. The settings allow me to include specific folders, exclude locations I don't need, and adjust options such as file size limits and supported file formats. Separate indexes for different document collections make it easier to keep personal files and work-related materials organized without moving them from their original locations.

5 tips you need to search more effectively in Windows File Explorer

Sift through your files easily

2
By  João Carrasqueira

Searching documents is more flexible than I expected

Boolean operators, wildcards, and fuzzy searches

DocFetcher stands out to me with the number of search options it offers without making the interface complicated. It supports more than basic keyword searches, which makes a noticeable difference when I'm looking for something specific. Boolean operators such as AND, OR, and NOT make searches more flexible by allowing me to combine or exclude specific terms. For example, a search can return documents containing one keyword while filtering out results that include another. It also supports wildcard searches, which are useful when I remember only part of a word or filename.

The preview pane is another feature I find genuinely useful. When I select a search result, DocFetcher displays a text preview of the document and highlights every matching keyword in yellow. The highlighted matches make it easy to jump between occurrences without reading the entire document. When the results are too broad, filters for document type, file location, and minimum or maximum file size help narrow down the search. There are also options for fuzzy searching, which finds words similar to my search term, and proximity searching, which finds two words appearing within a specified distance of each other. These options make it easier to find relevant results even when I don't remember the exact wording.

This free tool makes Windows' own search feel broken, and it's been free for nearly 20 years

I replaced my Windows search habit with this tiny tool, and I'm not looking back.

2
By  Yash Patel

Sometimes, simple tools get it right

DocFetcher doesn't have a modern interface or a fancy AI-powered feature set, and that's one of its biggest advantages. It stays grounded in what a desktop search utility should actually do instead of trying to be everything at once. There's no unnecessary complexity, subscription, or cloud dependency to worry about. Just a straightforward application that does its job reliably. While it may not look as polished as some newer alternatives, I appreciate that it focuses on functionality over flashy features.

DocFetcher

DocFetcher is a free, open-source, Java-based desktop search application that lets you search the full text of files on your computer.

item.title: My 12GB RTX 4070 Ti runs multiple DLSS 5 layers thanks to one OptiScaler setting
item.itunes:title: My 12GB RTX 4070 Ti runs multiple DLSS 5 layers thanks to one OptiScaler setting
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Ever since Nvidia finally released DLSS 5 for NBA 2K27, the neural rendering files have made their way to the open sea that is the internet. From there, the open-source and modding community has been hard at work injecting DLSS 5 into every possible game they could, and so have I.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I've effectively been giving all my old games free remasters with DLSS 5, and even the latest AAA titles feel incredibly more interesting with a neural rendering layer on. The problem, however, is that all of this neural magic comes with a brutal catch — performance.

The moment I turn DLSS 5 on, my RTX 4070 Ti starts paying the price, and every additional neural rendering pass makes that cost even harder to justify. Thankfully, OptiScaler has a deceptively simple feature, and it completely changes what I can get away with a 12GB GPU.

Stop calling it AI slop — upscaling is democratizing high-end gaming for the 99%

Better visuals for those not on the bleeding edge.

26
By  Samarveer Singh

OptiScaler is how I got DLSS 5 running on my RTX 4070 Ti

Spoofing Blackwell is only the beginning

Even when there are plenty of games in my Steam library that support 2x frame generation and regular DLSS 4.5 upscaling, I almost always use OptiScaler alongside most of them. That's simply because OptiScaler offers so many more features that regular titles simply do not. For starters, OptiScaler reports my RTX 4070 Ti as an RTX 50-series GPU to the game, which then unlocks multi-frame generation for me to use.

Similarly, it also allows me to use DLSS 5 and neural rendering in my titles, even if, on paper, that feature is reserved exclusively for 50-series cards. With a quick injection of OptiScaler and the right DLSS files, all that remains is to boot up a game, and see exactly how much neural rendering I can get away with before my GPU reaches its VRAM limit.

That's where things get iffy for me, since even a couple of neural rendering passes threaten to crash my game. After all, neural rendering is pretty VRAM heavy, and when you're running a game at High-to-Ultra graphics presets, along with ray tracing, at 1440p or 4K, you're already running close to the 12GB VRAM limit. With all these graphics features fighting one another for VRAM, I usually find myself stuck in the low 40 FPS territory as soon as I turn on neural rendering, and that's before I can even double down on the AI rendering.

I put DLSS 5 on my entire desktop, and it showed me neural rendering's real limits

DLSS 5 Live Flow promised to transform my desktop — here's what actually happened

3
By  Samarveer Singh

OptiScaler can move DLSS 5's place in the pipeline

That's how I regain half the framerate I lose

The biggest problem with stacking DLSS 5 neural rendering isn't really the first pass. It's what happens when I ask the GPU to do it again. That makes sense, too, since every neural rendering pass has to work on a full 1440p or 4K image. Thankfully, OptiScaler offers a nifty feature that allows you to move DLSS 5's neural pass in the pipeline.

Since every NR (neural rendering) pass has to work on an already-upscaled image, OptiScaler lets you use the "NR before SR" option, which flips that order, and makes neural rendering operate on the lower internal resolution image before SR (Super Resolution) upscales it to the target resolution.

Elden Ring (Frame-unlocked) Maximum + RT | RTX 4070 Ti + Ryzen 5 7600X + 32GB DDR5 RAM

Configuration

Average FPS

VRAM Usage

DLSS 4.5 Balanced

147 FPS

9.0 GB

DLSS 5 NR ×1 — After SR

71 FPS

10.1 GB

DLSS 5 NR ×1 — Before SR

98 FPS

9.8 GB

DLSS 5 NR ×2 — After SR

52 FPS

10.7 GB

DLSS 5 NR ×2 — Before SR

72 FPS

10.5 GB

DLSS 5 NR ×3 — After SR

42 FPS

11.8 GB

DLSS 5 NR ×3 — Before SR

61 FPS

11.5 GB

Truth be told, it sounds insultingly simple, but the performance difference is anything but. When I use neural rendering before Super Resolution's upscaling, my RTX 4070 Ti has far fewer pixels to chew through during the most expensive part of the pipeline. In my testing of Elden Ring, the first pass recovered roughly half of the performance I lost with conventional neural rendering.

If you've ever heard someone on the internet say that "DLSS 5 begins with the second pass," they're not exactly wrong. In all the gorgeous and transformative videos you see on the internet, those games are almost always running two or even three passes of neural rendering.

On my 12GB VRAM card, though, I can only stack a second neural-rendering layer through this OptiScaler feature. Otherwise, I'd be risking crashing my games or turning my RTX 4070 Ti into a space heater. Of course, the VRAM cost still rises while stacking another NR layer, but the overhead becomes manageable enough to experiment with.

Naturally, I was worried about the visual difference, but it still remains enormous, to say the very least. Vanilla rendering still looks noticeably flatter compared to the DLSS 5 version, even with NR moved ahead of Super Resolution. I'm simply doing the expensive work at a much friendlier resolution, which is exactly what makes this trick so useful.

Bloodborne and P.T. finally run on PC "natively," so I remastered them with DLSS 5

These abandoned classics deserved better

2
By  Samarveer Singh

Even RTX 50 series users don't have these tricks natively

Nvidia's newest GPUs still don't get these tricks

There's something particularly funny about all of this. I'm doing this on an RTX 4070 Ti, a GPU Nvidia would very much prefer I consider obsolete in the age of Blackwell. And yet, OptiScaler is giving me access to DLSS 5 features that even RTX 50-series owners don't get officially. I can change where neural rendering sits in the rendering pipeline instead of being locked into Nvidia's prescribed implementation.

Even the ability to stack multiple neural-rendering passes is not something that RTX 50-series users can enable in games like NBA 2K27 if they don't use OptiScaler. Nvidia's implementation gives you the neural-rendering effect, but it doesn't expose the same kind of control over how aggressively I can pile those passes onto an image.

I still know where my 4070 Ti stands, and I'm aware it isn't faster than a Blackwell GPU. This experiment, though, does expose just how software-defined DLSS 5 is. With the right DLLs, architecture spoofing, and a tool willing to poke around where Nvidia doesn't, a 12GB Ada Lovelace card can do some remarkably stupid things with technology supposedly reserved for newer hardware.

Before GTA 6 comes out, I'm playing the entirety of GTA 5 completely in my web browser

Ctrl+T for Los Santos.

By  Samarveer Singh

One open-source tool handed my GPU more power

It's deeply entertaining to squeeze more power out of my GPU, especially since Nvidia has already moved it into the rearview mirror. At this point, the VRAM is the only limitation of this last-gen GPU, since software seems to have removed every other limitation. If that sounds like an overstatement, then, at the very least, software has exposed just how much room there is between what a GPU physically supports and what the manufacturer has decided it should support.

That's why experiments like this are so compelling to me. DLSS 5 may have been designed around newer hardware, but the open-source community keeps finding ways to make those boundaries considerably less rigid.

item.title: 4 jobs my local AI handles for free that I would never trust with a cloud model
item.itunes:title: 4 jobs my local AI handles for free that I would never trust with a cloud model
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Lately, I've found myself ruminating about the privacy concerns surrounding sharing every bit of data with cloud AI service providers. I've previously talked about how AI chatbots, due to the nature of their platform, have access to far more user data than search engines ever did, and that makes them uniquely vulnerable. Frontier models are multimodal and take in text, images, documents, and even video, while a search engine only kept track of what a user was looking for.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Despite all of this, LLMs are useful to a wide range of people in a wide range of different tasks, and it would hurt many workflows if that capability were to go away tomorrow. Fortunately, there's a balanced approach that keeps the capability without sending any data to the cloud, and it's possible by using local models on my own hardware. Here are a few jobs my local LLM handles for me, so that none of my personally identifiable information is sent to a cloud provider's server.

Proofreading everything I type on my PC

Because my private emails shouldn't become anyone's training data

A strange aspect about cloud grammar-check services is that, over the past few years, many have become integrated with AI in one way or another, and more often than not, signing up for one of these services means unwittingly opting in to train a model.

A key issue with that is the fact that these services are quite pervasive, in that, most can run as browser extensions in every text box you open, silently training on what you type while correcting a stray apostrophe now and then. Before I wrote about tech, I worked in financial crime compliance at a major UK retail bank, and by banking governance criteria, that software would pass as a keylogger.

The one place where the use of such services bothers me the most is emails. They carry names, figures, and conversations that are sometimes confidential and meant for one person. That's why I've taken to proofreading mine with an open-source tool known as Writing Tools that routes the text to Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on my RTX 4070 Ti Super instead of a server I don't control.

I'm not paying $20 for ChatGPT or Claude because a free local LLM does everything I need

The bills disappeared, but the job gets done all the same

19
By  Abhinav Raj

Maintaining my PC with an agent

There's too much here a cloud server shouldn't see

Recently, I couldn't help but notice that it has become quite fashionable to let an agent and its sub-agents handle various tasks that many users consider tedious when it comes to PC maintenance. A lot of tech influencers and YouTubers like to showcase various capabilities of such agents running via Antigravity or Claude Code harnesses, but I've always found it worth thinking about how much information these apps relay to service providers, especially on personal computing devices.

At the same time, I also get the appeal of going fully hands-off when it comes to menial tasks like updating your apps to their latest versions by just dropping a prompt instead of manually chasing files yourself, and that is why I run Nemotron 3.5 Bolt through Hermes Agent on my own GPU. It has the power to get all of those tasks done, learn what it needs to about my machine, and load its notes into every session for ease of use, without any of that leaving my own network.

I don't pay for ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, or Claude – I stick to my self-hosted LLMs instead

There's no point in relying on AI tools when my local LLMs can handle everything

27
By  Ayush Pande

Vetting my documents and images for personally identifiable information

Everything can be made shareable with just a single prompt

Screenshots are a big part of how I show my work, and they're also where personal details can slip through. It could be an email address in the top left-hand corner of Windows Settings app, a Wi-Fi network name in Quick Settings, or a file name in a folder view that can end up in the public domain if I'm too lax with it. The catch is that checking a raw screenshot with a cloud model means uploading the very details I'm trying to keep private.

I imagine many other professions such as accounting and finance, as well as marketing and law, might have similar concerns surrounding client names and account details sitting in their documents. For me, the safest way to take a second look to see if there's anything I've missed is to feed the data to a local model served via llama.cpp, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B is the model I usually go to for this task which runs locally with its vision file.

I connected my local LLM to Gmail, Calendar, and Home Assistant, and it finally became useful

It can now actually be productive.

2
By  Anurag Singh

Making sense of my finances

It comes in really handy during tax season

Before local LLMs were a thing, I would dread the tax season, perhaps more so than the average person. There's quite a lot of issues surrounding making sense of your finances when the money you move between your bank accounts shows up twice, once coming in and once going out, and some transactions just miss your eye in the maze of a dozen similar transactions. The worst part is that your accountant needs every one of those lines matched and explained before anything gets filed.

My bank statements are about the most revealing documents I own, with balances, account numbers, and every person or business I've paid, so they're the last thing I would want on a cloud server. Those are all the hassles I do not have with a local model that can make sense of that ocean of information while running locally on my GPU, which can effortlessly parse and reconcile transactions across all my accounts, pair up the transfers, and flag anything it can't match so I can annotate it.

My local AI stack is saving my dollars, tokens, and my private data

My local LLM helps keep my personal and sensitive data private while aiding my productivity, and I believe I've established at least that much so far. However, an added advantage to complementing my workflow with a capable model such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B is that it helps me become less reliant on cloud services that charge monthly subscription fees for the same jobs, and so, it is also generally fiscally responsible to have a model on your drive that you can frequently offload some of your work to and save your tokens for the tasks that warrant them most.

item.title: Someone used Claude Code to make a sailing sim, then challenged other frontier LLMs to a race
item.itunes:title: Someone used Claude Code to make a sailing sim, then challenged other frontier LLMs to a race
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Claude Code sim lets LLMs helm virtual yachts using world-state inputs every 5s.
  • Gemini 4 Argon won easily; GPT-6 Astra 2nd, Claude Opus stalled, Qwen visited a beach.
  • The leading theory says Gemini's spatial awareness (for Maps/Earth) gave it an edge over the others.

If you gave Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon a yacht each, then told them to sail across a body of water and back with weather conditions, who do you think will win? While it'd be a very expensive project to do (both in terms of getting the boats and feeding each LLM with credits), someone has done the next best thing. They used Claude Code to make a realistic boat-racing simulator, then tasked the frontier LLM models with a virtual race.

Claude Code created a sailing arena for four AI models to duke it out

The results were wildly varied

Over on the ClaudeAI subreddit, user abhi3188 showed off what they made in Claude Code. It's a sailing simulator that allows an LLM to take the helm of a virtual yacht and sail back and forth across a body of water. As for the sailors, abhi3188 picked Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon, and Qwen 3.5-9B, the latter of which they admit they "threw it in there for fun."

Here's how the boat race worked:

Every 5 secs each model gets the full state of the world (23 raw numbers like heading, speed, wind, where the next mark is etc) and sets its helm and sails. No sailing tips. The sim pauses while it thinks, so slow models aren't punished.

As for the race, Qwen came in dead last as it seemingly refused to race and instead visited a nearby beach. Despite having a hand in coding the sim, Claude Opus 5.5 came in third after it stalled on the way home and timed out. GPT-6 Astra finished second after completing a full lap, and Gemini 4 Argon secured an easy win, at 1/5th of the cost in tokens versus Astra.

People speculated as to why Gemini was the superior sailor here, and a leading theory is that Google gave it superior spatial awareness because they also want to use it in Google Maps and Earth. Either way, I think I'd enjoy more of these AI duels. Battlebots, anyone?

I asked Google Antigravity to build a website, then let Claude Code redesign it

One AI built it, another reimagined.

9
By  Parth Shah

item.title: Someone got an offline LLM running on a 2015 Kindle Paperwhite, even if it’s quite slow
item.itunes:title: Someone got an offline LLM running on a 2015 Kindle Paperwhite, even if it’s quite slow
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Inkwell runs Alpine Linux on a jailbroken 2015 Kindle Paperwhite, with apps like Terminal, chess, and DOOM included.
  • Quill runs SmolLM2 via Llama.cpp entirely on-device, and nothing leaves the Kindle.
  • Smart mode slows output to ~0.7 wps, but the whole project is a neat revival for old e‑readers.

While we love our frontier LLMs here at XDA, we also have a soft spot for running local ones. As LLM tech advances, we're seeing models get more powerful, but we're also seeing people squeeze less powerful models onto older hardware. For instance, someone has gotten Quill running on a 2015 Kindle Paperwhite, and while it won't be replacing ChatGPT anytime soon, it's still an impressive feat.

Putting Alpine Linux on an 11-year-old Kindle is definitely a flex

The LLM is just the cherry on top

Credit: Pragyaan Gaur

As spotted by Hackaday, this cool project comes to us via Pragyaan Gaur on GitHub. It's called Inkwell, and the idea is that you can take a jailbroken Kindle Paperwhite from 2015 and run an Alpine Linux userspace built specifically for the e-ink device. There are some really fun features in Inkwell, such as a Terminal, a chess game, and, of course, DOOM runs on it. However, arguably its most impressive feature is its chatbot:

Quill is a chatbot that runs SmolLM2 through llama.cpp on the Kindle's own processor. It writes its answer word by word at about 1.7 words per second with the quick model, and a slower smart model can be added. Nothing leaves the device.

item.title: Windows has a hidden, free SSH server, and I manage every PC in my house from one terminal now
item.itunes:title: Windows has a hidden, free SSH server, and I manage every PC in my house from one terminal now
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Windows has had a built-in server for nearly a decade. SSH is a quintessential feature for anyone who uses more than one computer in their home, especially if they are into servers. I have multiple servers built out of old thin clients, laptops, WSL virtual machines, and single-board computers. I mostly manage everything from one of my Windows computers and never really gave a thought to using an SSH server on it.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The most obvious way to connect to any remote Windows machine is via a remote desktop tool, and SSH never felt useful. However, the GUI remote desktop version is not necessary at all times. When you are running some services and self-hosted tools on a Windows machine, the SSH server becomes useful. Windows lists OpenSSH as an optional feature, but it's now my favorite tool to control Windows PCs from the terminal.

OpenSSH is part of Windows

But only the client comes preinstalled

As someone who manages home servers and conducts self-hosting experiments regularly, SSH is absolutely unavoidable for me. I've never been a fan of SSH clients and prefer to use the built-in SSH tool on Windows. However, I had no idea I'd been using the OpenSSH client for so long on my main Windows PC. I always thought of OpenSSH as a third-party tool included with many Linux distributions. It never occurred to me that Windows integrates it by default.

If you've ever used SSH, you know that the client doesn't matter at all. You can connect to any other SSH tool, as I do, but the connection protocol, aka SSH, remains the same. For example, all my home servers use DietPi, and they have Dropbear as the default SSH server. But I don't have any problem controlling them from my OpenSSH CLI tool on Windows.

I tested dual-boot, WSL2, and VMs to run Linux apps on Windows, and only one was worth keeping

Dual-boot, VMs, and WSL2 walk into a Windows PC...

10
By  Ayush Pande

Similarly, I can control an OpenSSH server running on a Windows PC via a Linux system without facing connection challenges. SSH is a protocol, and the client doesn't matter. But I didn't know the OpenSSH server existed as an optional Windows feature.

Open Settings and go to Optional features to find the OpenSSH Server option. Select the checkbox, then click Install to add it to your Windows PC.

Remotely managing Windows systems

Just like any other SSH session

Accessing a Windows PC via SSH is a learning experience. You can use CLI tools like CMD and PowerShell from another system to control services and processes and view system information. I can launch PowerShell by typing its name and then use all the cmdlets it offers. Similarly, I can use other commands to view active processes, tweak network settings, or even force lock or reboot the system.

One lazy use case for running an OpenSSH server is when I’m on the lower floor and want to shut down the main or other Windows systems. I can start an SSH session from my Android phone, run the shutdown command, and sleep peacefully. I highly suggest using Termius as an Android SSH app because it can save profiles and has features that make the absence of a physical keyboard less painful.

This is just surface-level control of what anyone usually does with a server. However, there is a completely different use case, like using SSH to manage the WSL environment. I find it relatable because I run a Paperless-ngx server as a Docker container inside an Ubuntu WSL machine. It keeps working in the background and doesn't bother any user, especially my niece, who loves to play games and surf the web on it.

Microsoft is killing Remote Desktop: Use these 4 free alternatives instead

Microsoft is deprecating the Remote Desktop app (RDP) but there are still free alternatives you can use.

18
By  Brian Burgess

The laptop silently runs the server in the background, and I can gain complete control of the WSL machine by SSHing into it or the host (Windows PC). The latter is more powerful because I can reboot the machine and do more system-level troubleshooting, which is not possible with SSH access to just the WSL machine.

I can do more exciting things with the Paperless-ngx instance. One of them is adding a local LLM to help find, label, and organize things. The SSH session feels no different from controlling WSL via PowerShell; I can modify the containers and add new ones. I can even update my host system’s packages using Winget and spin up new WSL machines, if necessary.

Remote desktop is useful

But it's not applicable everywhere

Some things are best left to the terminal, and WSL is one of those components for me. There’s no reason to use a remote desktop app for a GUI session when my work is CLI-based. Even if I don’t have a visual connection to the target Windows PC, I can still use PowerShell cmdlets in my SSH sessions for basic actions. The only caveat is that you must know your way around the terminal to make SSH sessions feel useful.

Microsoft retired the built-in Remote Desktop app, and unless the target system has the Pro edition of Windows, the tool was partially useful. Windows Home users could only use the tool to connect to other RDP servers but lacked the option to host one. An OpenSSH server has no such restrictions and doesn’t offer features based on Windows editions. It’s a way to create an SSH server and supports cross-platform connections.

Everything is interconnected

I can control my Linux system from Windows and vice versa via any terminal now. Even my phone can connect to all these systems and manage Windows PCs as well. OpenSSH server is free to use and very easy to set up. You only need to allow incoming connections through Windows Firewall, and you never need to configure it again. SSH sessions are the backbone of any remote server management, and my Windows PCs feel no different from the Linux home servers now. To access the Windows PC outside the network, you can install Tailscale on the host machine.

But as someone who has spent the last couple of months pushing my outdated hardware to its limits, I must admit that the majority of my productivity needs are easily met by local LLMs running on my home lab nodes. In fact, between my self-hosted repertoire of productivity apps and lightweight agent harnesses, I’ve got a decent collection of services that rely on my local AI models.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

My clipboard assistant is one such addition to this suite. And despite sounding like a simple tool, it lets me run analysis tasks on copied elements, translate text in different languages, and run OCR workloads on screenshots – all without forcing me to spend a dime on premium subscription fees or sending my data to external servers.

I'm not paying $20 for ChatGPT or Claude because a free local LLM does everything I need

The bills disappeared, but the job gets done all the same

19
By  Abhinav Raj

Sirius AI Tray Assistant is the local tool that connects to my clipboard

While Gemma 4 E4B serves as the brain of this setup

Seeing as how my clipboard assistant would gain access to every piece of text I’d end up copying during my everyday tasks, I wanted to use something that respects my privacy and doesn’t phone home for simple inference tasks. After sifting through different community-created tools, I eventually came across the Sirius AI Tray Assistant repo by developer Zoott28354, and it seemed like the perfect companion for my self-hosted clipboard manager. But before I go over how I use it in my setup, let me quickly discuss the LLM powering this app: Gemma 4 E4B (Q4_K_M). Since it has an effective parameter size of 4.5B, it’s light enough to run on pretty much any GPU in my arsenal.

Better yet, it runs at a break-neck pace on my outdated graphics cards – to the point that my RTX 3080 Ti manages to hit well over 110+ tokens/second for this LLM. For a clipboard analysis tool, where I’d rather not wait several minutes for the inference tasks to wrap up, the Gemma 4 E4B + RTX 3080 Ti combo meshes really well for my productivity tasks.

Pairing my local LLM with Sirius AI Tray Assistant was just as easy. Once I’d downloaded this clipboard companion, I opened the Configuration button within its tray menu, chose llama.cpp as the server, and used the http://localhost:8080/v1 link as the Gemma 4 E4B host.

That said, I’ve also tinkered with remote connections here, as I can’t always spare my daily driver’s GPU for LLM inference tasks. And as long as I use a Custom server profile and add the IP address pointing to the llama-server running on my Proxmox-powered LXC, I can still use the other GPUs in my arsenal to drive the clipboard inference operations on the Sirius Assistant.

I don't pay for ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, or Claude – I stick to my self-hosted LLMs instead

There's no point in relying on AI tools when my local LLMs can handle everything

27
By  Ayush Pande

Custom clipboard prompts make this setup a godsend for productivity

And the persistent memory retains important analysis tasks

By default, the analysis option within the Sirius AI Tray Assistant’s menu uses my Gemma 4 E4B instance to convert the contents of my clipboard to English and generates a detailed analysis on their utility, which is pretty impressive in its own right. But what makes this tool a powerhouse for handling everyday tasks is the custom prompt window, where I can freely tweak the analysis operation to suit my use case.

For example, I often need to remove formatting when I grab PowerShell scripts, Linux commands, and random code snippets when I document my projects. Well, adding the “Clear formatting” instruction as the custom prompt for my text searches gets the job done. Speaking of code, I’ve configured this AI app to go over the commands, snippets, and scripts I often copy from documentation, and all I have to do is click on the Analyze text option to get a brief summary of what it can do.

Likewise, if I’m researching something in a different language, I can leave the “translate to English” prompt enabled and wait a few seconds for the Sirius + Gemma 4 E4B combo to work its magic. And for tasks where I may need to consult my clipboard contents, I can always access the persistent chat logs on Sirius AI.

It’s pretty handy for running OCR tasks on screenshots

Aside from my copied text, Sirius Assistant can even look into the screenshots I create using the Windows Snipping Tool, and it works well with Gemma 4 E4B because the LLM ships with image analysis capabilities. For example, if I’ve got text that I can't copy with the ol’ reliable Ctrl + C shortcut, I can just take its screenshot using the Windows Snipping Tool and have Sirius + Gemma 4 E4B create an OCR report highlighting it – provided the text in question is somewhat readable and isn’t a pixelated mess, of course.

The Sirius AI Tray Assistant has become my newest work companion

Considering that I don’t need a bulky GPU or pay huge to drive the Sirius Assistant, it meshes well with the outdated systems in my home lab. In fact, I’ve even tested it with Gemma 4 E4B instances running on my GTX 1060 laptop and GTX 1080-powered llama.cpp LXC, and both setups are fast enough for everyday tasks. Combine that with the fact that everything runs locally, and you can see why I’ve installed it across all the Windows machines in my arsenal.

It's hard to ignore the fact that 4K monitors are having a bit of a moment. If you're looking to upgrade your workspace without breaking the bank, look no further than the Acer ProDesigner 4K Monitor, currently down to $300 on Amazon. It delivers fantastic color accuracy and plenty of resolution for daily productivity, media consumption, and entry-level creative work.

What's so great about the Acer ProDesigner 4K Monitor?

Incredible visuals and color accuracy

When it comes to the panel, you're looking at a display that prioritizes color fidelity over flashy refresh rates. That fantastic color accuracy means you get true-to-life hues right out of the box—a massive upgrade over the washed-out panels on cheaper alternatives. Whether you're color-grading photos, editing video, or just trying to get crisp text for spreadsheets, the 4K resolution gives you the pixel density needed to make everything look sharp.

Beyond the picture quality, you get the connectivity options that modern setups demand. You can plug in your desktop or laptop via standard HDMI and DisplayPort inputs, ensuring compatibility with just about any machine you own. There's also the ability to easily daisy-chain additional peripherals, which is fantastic if your workflow requires multiple devices plugged in at once.

While it isn't designed for the likes of competitive eSports, the panel's 144Hz response rate is perfectly adequate for casual gaming and smooth desktop navigation. You can also mount it on a standard VESA arm for a cleaner desk layout, and the adjustable stand lets you tilt it to match your exact viewing angle. This makes it a solid foundation for a dual-monitor setup or as a primary display for anyone who values clarity over high frame rates.

By  Tanveer Singh

For those who need a reliable secondary screen or a primary display for work-from-home setups, this monitor offers excellent value. The color accuracy ensures that your images and videos look professional, while the 4K resolution provides the workspace real estate needed for multitasking. You can run multiple windows side by side without feeling cramped, making it ideal for coding, writing, or financial analysis.

Right now, you can grab the Acer ProDesigner 4K Monitor for just $300. Give it a look if you want to upgrade your workspace without paying a premium for features you won't actually use.

item.title: Tdarr shrank my media library by a third, and I can't tell the difference on my TV
item.itunes:title: Tdarr shrank my media library by a third, and I can't tell the difference on my TV
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My NAS holds a large movie library, plus backups, documents, and other files, and I’d like to keep it all. Buying a new drive in 2026 is a pipe dream, so I’d rather make the most of the storage I already have. That means finding ways to make my movies take up less space without ruining how they look on my TV.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I am using Tdarr to do that. It handles that job by automatically re-encoding files using settings you choose. You point it at your library, set the rules, and let it work through the movies instead of converting each one manually. It shrank my library by roughly a third, and I can’t tell the difference when I watch the converted files on my TV.

Getting Tdarr to work through the library

You decide what gets converted

The movies on your NAS don’t necessarily use the same video codec or encoding settings, even when they share the same resolution. That gives you room to reduce their size without dropping a 4K movie to 1080p. HEVC, also called H.265, compresses video more efficiently than H.264, making older H.264 files useful candidates for conversion.

You could handle those conversions individually with HandBrake, but working through a large collection would get tedious. Tdarr uses FFmpeg or HandBrake to process files according to your rules, so you don’t have to keep adding movies to a queue yourself.

The setup has two parts – a server that manages the library and a node that does the encoding. Both can run on the same machine, or you can put the node on another computer. The latter is useful when your NAS holds the movies, but you want a more capable computer to handle the conversions. You also assign a cache folder where Tdarr can write its temporary output.

From there, you choose the encoder and quality settings. Those settings matter more than chasing the smallest possible file. If you push the compression too far, it removes detail, and one quality value won’t produce the same result across different encoders.

For an initial test, I used copies of a few movies and kept the originals available for comparison. You want to preserve the resolution and retain the audio tracks and subtitles you use, then check the output before letting Tdarr replace anything. Once you’re happy with those samples, you have a configuration worth applying to more of the library.

After years of ripping my 4K Blu-rays to Jellyfin, I’ve finally perfected my setup

My 4K Blu-ray ripping strategy to Jellyfin didn't happen overnight.

4
By  Brian Burgess

The smaller files still look good on my TV

The storage savings are easier to spot

I had more than 8TB of media in my library, and Tdarr freed up TBs of space without removing the movies themselves. That’s the overall saving across the collection, though individual files won’t all shrink by the same percentage. The source video and encoding settings determine how much space each conversion saves. For example, grainy footage needs more data to preserve its detail than a cleaner image.

It's not just the storage that I saved – I can’t tell the difference on my TV, and that makes the reduction worth it for me. Re-encoding with lossy settings does discard information, so I’m not claiming the converted files preserve every detail of the originals. I’m saying that whatever difference exists hasn’t made itself obvious when I watch them.

If you try this yourself, look beyond a bright, relatively still scene. Look for banding in dark backgrounds and gradients, compression artifacts during fast movement, and any loss of grain or fine texture. Those are more useful checks than opening the file properties and confirming that the output still says 4K.

Tdarr can keep working as the library grows

New additions get the same treatment

Tdarr can also watch your media folders for additions and process them using the rules you’ve already configured. Just make sure those rules also tell Tdarr when to leave a file alone. You can skip videos already in your chosen codec to prevent unnecessary repeat conversions.

Files that are already small deserve some consideration, too, since another encode costs processing time and discards more information without guaranteeing a worthwhile reduction. Also, since HDR and Dolby Vision files need settings that preserve the relevant metadata, I wouldn’t send them through an untested configuration.

Tdarr even lets you choose processing windows and limit how many workers run at once. If encoding competes with your backups or makes the computer sluggish during the day, you can move those jobs to quieter hours. You can also build checks into the workflow before it replaces an original. A size check can reject an output larger than its source, and a thorough health check can scan the video for decoding errors.

There’s still room for other cleanup tools alongside Tdarr. I previously recovered 900GB with Krokiet by reviewing duplicates and redundant movie releases.
